claim: Overtly sexual ad imagery roughly halved correct brand recall in Lindstrom's study (9.8% vs about 20% for men; 10.85% vs 22.3% for women).
body: Lindstrom calls this the Vampire Effect: a highly sexual or extremely attractive model pulls attention away from the brand name, logo and product, so viewers remember the ad but not who it was for. In his test, men shown sexual ads named the correct brand or product 9.8% of the time versus almost 20% for neutral versions; women 10.85% versus 22.3%. He pairs it with a 2001 Market Facts survey where 53% said they were more likely to buy when an ad showed images of love versus 26% for images alluding to sex, and argues people identify more with models who look like them. How to apply in ecommerce creative: when a hook relies on an attractive body or provocative image, check that the product and brand are on screen in the same frame and named early; test a version where the person is relatable rather than idealised; and measure brand recall or branded search lift, not only thumb-stop rate, because attention that does not attach to the brand is wasted. Category exceptions exist where the attractive body is the product benefit (underwear, swimwear, fragrance), and Lindstrom notes Calvin Klein sold heavily with provocative ads, so the risk is recall loss, not automatic sales loss.
conditions: Awareness and prospecting creative where brand recall matters; categories where the model is not the product benefit.
fails_when: The attractive body is itself the product promise (lingerie, swimwear, fitness transformation), or controversy is the strategy and reach outweighs recall; the figures come from a single commercially run study and may not replicate.

claim: In a saturated niche, test an unclaimed buyer (e.g. parents of kids with braces, not adults whitening teeth) as an angle in native image ads before building any advertorial.
body: The operator lost money in teeth whitening while targeting the same top desires as competitors (coffee stains, enamel), and reports high CPMs and weak conversion. The fix was to change who the ad speaks to, not the product: parents worried about white spots on a child's teeth during braces, with a cost-of-inaction frame (wasting about 6,000 on orthodontics). Reported results on that angle: about 1,000 spend, 160 add-to-carts, 16 cost per purchase and about 6x ROAS in one campaign; another ad set showed 4x to 13x ROAS on about 1,600 spend; CPMs fell to around 20; peak days around 5,000 in revenue. Sequence: 1) List distinct buyer types for the product, not only pain points. 2) Run them as about five angles in one CBO campaign with broad targeting, automatic placements and no cost caps, using long-form-copy native image ads (about 10 images). 3) Prefer a format competitors are not using (native image where rivals run video). 4) Only once one angle clearly wins, write an advertorial for that angle and scale it in a separate campaign. 5) Make new variations of the winner with fresh images. Revenue claims are self-reported by a dropshipper, so treat figures as anecdote.

fails_when: The niche is uncrowded, where top desires still convert and splitting into narrow angles slows learning; or the unclaimed buyer is too small a market, or targets minors or health conditions in ways that breach Meta ad policy.

claim: Open a video ad with your own take on a viral oddly-satisfying clip, then cut to the product at the payoff; Clemens says it out-watched product-first openings.
body: Clemens describes an ad for one of his ecommerce brands built from a TikTok trend: a glass bottle of marbles rolling down concrete stairs, clinking, cracking and spilling marbles, the kind of oddly satisfying clip that routinely draws around 10 million views. His team recreated that opening, then at the moment of the smash the video switched to the product. He reports that far more people watched it than versions that opened on the product, while admitting it is a complete bait-and-switch. His explanation is that people are drawn to physical cause-and-effect: things breaking, cutting, falling and sounding right, the same pull behind classic demonstrations like Otis cutting an elevator cable or a sword slicing a bullet. How to apply: pick a currently popular satisfying or physics-style format on the platform, film your own version (do not reuse someone else's footage), and make the switch happen at the moment of highest tension so the product feels like the payoff. Best when the product itself can be shown doing something physical (strength, sealing, cutting, absorbing). Measure hold rate at 3 seconds and thruplay against your product-first control, and check that the post-click conversion rate holds up, because borrowed attention can bring curious viewers rather than buyers.
conditions: Short-form video placements (TikTok, Reels, Shorts) with sound on; products that can be demonstrated physically; trend formats still current.
fails_when: Trend has gone stale; platform policies or audiences punish misleading openings (lower quality ranking, negative feedback); the gap between hook and product is so wide that clicks do not convert; premium brands whose trust depends on straightforward creative.

claim: Anchor the big idea's 'why now' to a fear that has reached the early or late majority (microplastics, seed oils), not one still fringe or already stale.
body: The reviewer builds a big idea from three overlapping inputs: what is unique in the product (for each component, argue why it has to be exactly this, such as why a liquid dropper and not a capsule), what the market currently believes and debates, and which prospect segment is targeted. The market input is read with the technology adoption curve: ideas move from innovators and early adopters to early majority, late majority and laggards, as keto and carnivore diets did. Marketers see trends early, so they risk building on ideas the mass market is not ready for, which reads as esoteric, or on ideas so old they bore. The sweet spot is an idea now in the early to late majority with plenty of momentum and published coverage, which in his 2025 view included microplastics and seed oils. That idea supplies the why now: the problem is worse today and not your fault, which gives urgency and a fresh epiphany. He also gives the mechanism a memorable characterisation (silk syrup, mulberry drops) and spends time on that name. How to apply: list three to five current health or lifestyle concerns your buyers recognise, judge each on the curve, and link only those your product can credibly connect to.
conditions: Direct-response creative for consumables in trend-sensitive categories (wellness, food, beauty); time-sensitive, judged at the moment of writing.
fails_when: Fear-based trend hooks without evidence that the product addresses that cause invite FTC and platform action; a trend that has passed into the laggard stage feels stale; brand-led premium positioning may reject fear angles.

claim: A founder ad does not need the founder on camera: run the same script as founder voice, founder evidence, a proxy (employee, dietitian, supplier) or founder-absent animation.
body: The agency describes a ladder of founder involvement, each step a different format carrying the same concept. Top: the founder on camera speaking. Next: founder voice only, over B-roll, animation or creator footage. Then founder evidence: photos of the founder in the lab, with certificates, or walking the factory facing away from camera. Then a founder proxy: an employee, a credentialed expert such as a dietitian, or the supplier tells the founder story; less effective than the founder but workable. Last: the founder absent, with the story told end to end through AI animation or claymation, which can show the problem visually (inside the body, at cell level) in a way talking heads cannot. The host ranks VSLs and founder ads as the highest lifetime-revenue single ads he has seen, and groups animation and claymation with VSLs as a rising format. How to apply: write one script, then produce it at three or four levels of this ladder to add format diversity without new concepts; use the lower rungs when the founder is camera-shy, private, or too senior for regular shoots; keep claims identical across versions so the proof still holds.

fails_when: Proxy or animation versions lose the authority that made the story credible (claims that only a founder or expert can make); AI animation that looks generic or breaches ad policy for health claims.

claim: Across an agency's top 15 founder ads by spend, the winning script ran adversarial claim, proof of claim, mechanism via founder story, proof of mechanism, then CTA with social proof.
body: Blue Sense Digital, which reports about $400M a year in Meta spend under management, had an AI model pull every founder ad in its business managers, watch them, extract scripts and rank them by lifetime spend and performance. The most common structure among the top 15 opens with a large adversarial claim ('the category is lying to you', 'supermarket X is full of plastic'), which doubles as the hook. Proof of that claim follows at once, such as a study showing competitor creatine gummies hold a fraction of the stated dose. The agency says no founder ad in the pull performed with a claim alone. Next comes the unique mechanism, told as the founder story (so I built it differently, here is how), then proof of the mechanism (factory visits, third-party tests, the clean ingredient label), and finally the CTA with offer, urgency and customer social proof. The story must be told through the viewer's problem, not the founder's biography: viewers keep watching because they recognize their own problem, and a curiosity gap that the founder solved it carries them to the mechanism. How to apply: write the claim and its proof first, and if you cannot prove the claim, choose another claim. Never invent a founder story.
conditions: DTC brands with a real founder origin tied to the product problem; cold and problem-aware audiences on Meta; categories where a competitor or industry practice can be credibly challenged.
fails_when: No provable adversarial claim exists, or claims about competitors create legal or policy risk (comparative claims, health claims); the founder story has no link to the buyer's problem; brands where the founder is a poor fit for the persona.

claim: Batch founder ads as 10 hooks x 3 bodies = 30 ads from about 5 minutes of recording; one 1 to 2 hour shoot covers 3 to 4 months.
body: The agency treats founder ads as a production pipeline, not one-off videos. Write 10 hooks and 3 materially different bodies, then pair every hook with every body: 30 ads. Recording takes about 4 to 5 minutes of camera time on a teleprompter; the real work, which the host puts at '99%', is scripting and ideation before the camera rolls. Adding two CTA endings would double it to 60, but the host rarely tests CTAs because average watch time falls off long before the end. With scripts and editing handled by a team or agency, a founder can shoot hundreds of ads in a one to two hour block, enough for three to four months; some clients ship 200 to 400 ads a month with a one or two person content team. To keep scripts fresh, separate static story elements (origin, the founder's personal problem, why the company started), which must stay consistent, from renewable ones: new reviews, one-star reviews, support inbox emails, supplier calls and product changes, in-person complaints. Pipe these into a store (an AI pull of the support inbox weekly) so a monthly scripting session has material. The example target is 40 founder ads a month inside a broader creative mix. Founders new to camera tend to sound robotic for their first hours on camera; let them speak from a sentence outline instead of a teleprompter.
conditions: Brands with a founder willing to shoot periodically and someone to script and edit; Meta accounts needing steady creative volume.
fails_when: No scriptwriter or editor, so the founder carries all the work; hooks written for volume that do not bridge into the body; a founder who stays stiff on camera, which makes the format underperform regardless of volume.

claim: Brands running $20M to $30M a year off one founder ad and its hook swaps decayed when it fatigued; keep founder ads as one portfolio weight.
body: Founder ads can carry a business: the host has seen single founder concepts, with their hook swaps and variants, drive $20M to $30M of revenue for DTC brands. The risk shows up when the concept fatigues. Many such brands reached the agency only after the fact: a year of revenue rode on one ad, the target market had all seen it, and the brand kept making near-copies of the same concept, which could not recover performance while no other formats were live. The business then decayed. The agency's rule is portfolio theory for creative: when founder ads work, lean in and make more, but do not overweight them; keep statics, sales and offer ads, animation and other formats live and spending, so another format can take over when the founder concept tires. There is also an exit angle: if founder ads hold most spend, buyers may flag key-person dependency in a term sheet. How to apply: report spend share by concept and format weekly; set a ceiling on any single concept's share; keep at least a few non-founder formats spending at all times even if their ROAS is lower; and plan the next concept while the current winner is still strong.
conditions: DTC brands scaling on Meta where one creative concept holds most spend; founder-led brands considering an exit.
fails_when: Very early brands still searching for a first working concept, where concentration is unavoidable; markets large enough that a concept's reach is far from saturated.
numbers: single founder concepts driving $20M to $30M revenue in a year

claim: Build founder-ad concepts from a matrix of persona, awareness stage, angle, offer, proof type and founder role; changing any one cell gives a new concept.
body: A founder story is finite, so diversity must come from the variables around it. The agency's matrix: persona, awareness stage, angle, offer, proof type and the founder's role. Its top-performing combination: a skeptical first-time category buyer at problem awareness, the 'whole category is lying' angle, a single SKU, a lab certificate as proof, founder as protagonist. Second: an existing category buyer (solution aware), a dosage angle (competitors under-dose), a bundle justified because a companion product makes the first work, a competitor teardown as proof. Third: a gift buyer at product awareness, a taste angle, a gift pack, a read-aloud customer email as proof. Founder roles go beyond the protagonist ('I built this'), which nearly all founder ads use: witness ('a customer emailed me last week'), interviewer ('I asked our lab why'), reader ('I just got a one-star review, let me read it'). Swapping roles across three concepts gives four versions each; swapping offers multiplies again, reaching 20 to 30 ads. Persona is hardest to change when the founder does not resemble the buyer; re-angle the true story (a creatine founder who got his mother to take gummies opens older women). Role swapping matters most for six- and seven-figure brands making content in-house; at eight figures and up, hand these scripts to others to save founder time.
conditions: Brands with a genuine founder story and one or more SKUs; Meta accounts that need concept diversity, not only format diversity.
fails_when: Inventing story details to fit a persona (the host calls it black hat and an exit-value risk); a founder who visibly cannot represent the buyer; brands with only one true angle, where angle changes run out quickly.

claim: Premium brands can open with lo-fi footage safely if the product is kept out of the lo-fi section; it then reads as contrast, not cheap association.
body: A common worry is that low-fidelity footage cheapens a premium brand. The host's teardown of a premium electric toothbrush ad shows the workaround: the first half, shot lo-fi, covers the founder's team buying every top-rated competitor, finding porous plastic and mouldy charging bases, and agitating the hygiene problem, all without showing their own product. Only in the last 20 seconds do high-end shots of the aluminium brush appear. Because the product never appears inside the rough footage, viewers do not link it with low quality; the jump in production value instead sets it apart from the competitors shown in the lo-fi section. A related point from another teardown: showing the product in the first two or three seconds tells viewers they are watching an ad, and cutting away to product B-roll mid-story breaks attention. How to apply: script the problem and competitor sections for lo-fi, story-first shooting; hold the product reveal until the mechanism; switch to premium visuals at the reveal; keep the founder on screen while the story runs and save product B-roll for later.
conditions: Premium-positioned products on paid social using founder or UGC-style openings; problem-agitation scripts with a delayed reveal.
fails_when: Impulse or visual products where showing the product working in the first seconds is the hook (cleaning demos, gadgets); very short placements where a delayed reveal never gets watched.
numbers: premium product shots held to the final ~20 seconds in the example

claim: Put most ads in awareness stages 1 to 3 and about 20% in stages 4 and 5; founder ads opening on product benefits will not scale cold.
body: The host uses the five stages of awareness to judge whether an ad can take spend. An ad that introduces the product in the first line, lists ingredients or says 'it tastes great and saves money' speaks to people who are already product aware. That messaging is objection handling for buyers near purchase, useful at the bottom of the funnel, but a cold, unaware viewer has no reason to care. His examples: a skincare founder ad opening with compliments on her oil and customer photos is a stage-four ad, fine for converting warm prospects but a poor home for $250k of cold spend; a supplement drink's ad library built almost entirely on its founder's personal brand and low-funnel claims will struggle to scale because cold viewers do not know who he is. How to apply: tag every ad with its awareness stage before launch; aim for most of the mix in unaware, problem-aware and solution-aware stages (problem agitation, education, mechanism), and about 20% in product-aware and most-aware stages (testimonials, price and taste reassurance, offers); if an account cannot scale, check whether its winners all sit at stage four or five.
conditions: Meta accounts using broad targeting where the same ads must reach cold and warm users; brands trying to grow beyond existing demand.
fails_when: Small accounts with strong existing awareness (a famous founder, a viral product) where product-aware ads still find enough buyers; retargeting-only budgets.
numbers: ~80% of ads in awareness stages 1 to 3, ~20% in stages 4 and 5

claim: Reshooting a fatigued founder ad with the same script in a new setting (outside instead of inside the gym) let it absorb about $40,000 more spend.
body: A founder's face is the strongest sameness signal in an account: talking-head founder videos shot in one spot look alike to the delivery system and get served to the same people, so they fatigue fast. The agency's fix is format variation before concept change. In one account, the same script, editing and B-roll, reshot outside the gym instead of inside, took a fatigued ad and carried roughly another $40,000 of spend. The host says reusing scripts is fine even under Andromeda as long as editing or scenery differ enough. As founder-ad volume grows, the changes must get bigger: a new set, a walk through a store aisle handling competitor products, an organic-style format such as a tier list, or animation. Two cameras, motion, fast cuts and overlays are the minimum; a phone-propped talking head rarely works unless the founder is famous. How to apply: during any founder shoot, move location several times so one script yields several visually distinct versions; when a winner fatigues, reshoot it in a new scene before writing a new concept; and track whether the new version gets fresh reach or the same audience.
conditions: Meta accounts running several founder talking-head ads; winning scripts that fatigue on frequency rather than message.
fails_when: The concept itself is exhausted across the target market (everyone has seen the story), which a scene change cannot fix; very small markets where reach saturates quickly.

claim: Run 2 to 4 hook variants per body (up to 8); 20 to 40 hooks on one body spreads budget too thin for ads to exit learning.
body: Most viewers never get past the hook, so swapping it is the cheapest way to turn a losing ad into a winner or to extend a winner: the host says reshooting the hook in new places is one of the easiest ways to keep a high-performing founder ad alive, and that hook variation still works under Meta's Andromeda delivery system. The limit is quality and budget. Only a handful of hooks can bridge naturally into a given body, so most bodies support two to four strong hooks, sometimes up to eight. The agency has launched one body with 9 and even 40 hook variants, and found the wide spread inefficient: with, say, $1,000 a day behind a founder-ad test, splitting it across 20 to 40 near-identical ads starves each of the conversions needed to exit the learning phase and produce readable data. How to apply: for each body, write only the hooks that make contextual sense into its first line; launch two to four; when an ad works, add new hooks shot in different settings rather than new bodies; and check that each hook's promise is paid off in the body. Testing CTAs is low value because few viewers reach them.

fails_when: Very large budgets that can fund many variants to significance; static or carousel ads where the 'hook' is the headline; hooks that do not bridge to the body, which raise thumb-stop but cut conversion.

claim: After a strong problem hook, add 4 to 6 more seconds of mechanism education before naming the product; jumping straight to the product was blamed for one ad's flop.
body: The bridge is the line that moves from the hook and problem into the product. In the creatine gummy ad, the hook was strong: heat in manufacturing destroys the creatine, which matches a story buyers had already heard about gummies testing near zero. The ad then jumped straight to 'that's why I started taking' the brand, and the reviewer blames that abrupt bridge for a weak result (three likes after a couple of weeks of running). His fix is one or two lines of the founder's own search, such as researching suppliers directly, before the product appears. In the IM8 gut-health VSL, which he rates as the best of the five, he still sees an aggressive bridge and suggests 4 to 6 more seconds explaining why probiotics alone fail (prebiotics and postbiotics are also needed) before introducing the all-in-one product. The mechanism is that a viewer who has just accepted a problem needs to accept the reason for the solution before they accept a brand; skipping that step reads as a pitch and they leave. Use it as a review check: find the first mention of the brand and ask what the viewer must believe beforehand.
conditions: Problem-aware or unaware cold traffic; educational and VSL-style video ads for supplements and wellness.
fails_when: Product-aware retargeting audiences who already know the mechanism, where extra education slows the path to the offer.

claim: An attention-grab hook (a knife in the product) followed by a feature-heavy body is a mismatch: the hook pulls cold viewers while the body only serves people ready to buy.
body: The teardown's first rule: a hook's job is to call in the right viewer for the stage of awareness the rest of the ad serves, not to stop everyone. In the critiqued nootropic ad, a weird visual opens the video, the kind of hook only used to grab any viewer at the top of the funnel. The body then lists ingredients, nanoencapsulation and absorption claims, which only interests product-aware viewers close to purchase. Cold viewers drop off once the features start, and warm viewers were never called in by the hook, so the ad serves nobody well; the practitioner also argues an unqualified audience gives the platform's delivery poor signals about who to find. A protein-shaker ad shows the same pattern in milder form. How to apply it: before scripting, decide which awareness stage the ad is for (unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, most aware). For product-aware ads, open with the product, offer or a named benefit. For cold, problem-aware ads, open with a pain or a surprising claim tied to the problem, then educate. Review each finished ad by asking whether the opening and the next 20 seconds are aimed at the same person.
conditions: Paid social video ads (Meta feed and Reels) for DTC products, especially supplements and wellness.
fails_when: Products with broad, impulse appeal where almost any viewer is a prospect, so a pure attention hook followed by a quick product pitch can still sell.

claim: Ban 'it's not X, it's Y' lines (contrast negation) in AI-written ad scripts; viewers read the pattern as AI copy.
body: While praising the IM8 ad, the reviewer flags the line 'your gut isn't broken, it's starving' as contrast negation: the 'it is not X, it is Y' construction that large language models overuse. He calls it a giveaway that a script was written by AI, along with stock analogies such as 'sending a single soldier into a war zone'. Because many brands now script with AI, these patterns repeat across feeds and make an ad feel generic at the moment it needs to feel native and specific. His practical rule: when you have Claude or another model draft scripts, add an explicit instruction to never use contrast negation, then reread the draft for other telltale constructions and swap them for concrete statements about the product or customer. This is a style rule, not a performance-tested result; the source offers no data, and the ad that used the line was still the reviewer's favourite of the five.

claim: Pitching a mass-market supplement only to serious athletes shrinks the addressable market; lead with benefits the sedentary majority wants (sleep, brain health) instead.
body: In the creatine ad, the brand says its product is not for the everyday sedentary crowd but for serious athletes. The reviewer argues this is the wrong angle for a supplement brand that wants to scale: most of the population is sedentary, so excluding them caps the market, and he doubts an elite-athlete-only brand in a market the size of Australia can grow very large. Elite athletes are also hard buyers: coaches control what they take and compliance rules restrict products. They also know the details, so loose wording backfires; the ad lists electrolytes and magnesium as separate ingredients, and an informed athlete knows magnesium is an electrolyte. His alternative: sell creatine's broader benefits, such as coping with less sleep and brain health, to everyone, gym or not, while checking each claim is compliant. The general test: if the angle excludes the largest group of likely buyers, it should be a deliberate niche bet, not a default.
conditions: Mass-market supplements and wellness products whose benefits apply beyond the niche named in the ad; brands aiming to scale paid social.
fails_when: Premium or performance brands whose edge is credibility with a specialist niche, or small markets where owning a narrow segment is the whole strategy.

claim: When a hook names an unfamiliar condition, immediately add a prevalence line (40% have it, most do not know) and call out several symptoms so viewers include themselves.
body: In the IM8 gut-health ad, which the reviewer rates highest, the opening calls out three groups at once (IBS, leaky gut, bloating) instead of one, which widens who stops to watch. When the script then names the underlying condition, dysbiosis, it immediately says around 40% of people have it and most do not know. The reviewer's point: naming a technical condition alone makes most viewers think the word is unfamiliar and does not apply to them, and they scroll. A prevalence statement plus a 'you might be among them' line turns an obscure label into a personal possibility and keeps a large audience. The same ad then stacks clinical claims (for example 85% reporting better digestion in a 12-week trial) as credibility. How to use it: when your mechanism rests on a condition or deficiency, open with the everyday symptoms people already notice, then name the cause, then state how common it is and that it usually goes unnoticed. Check that any prevalence figure and trial statistic you use is real, sourced and allowed under the category's advertising rules.
conditions: Health, wellness and supplement ads that rest on a named condition or mechanism; cold problem-aware audiences.
fails_when: Regulated claims where implying a viewer has a medical condition breaks platform or advertising policy; or when no credible prevalence data exists.

claim: A static headline must be fully clear or deliberately curious; the middle loses. Curiosity statics need an educational lander (listicle, advertorial), clear ones can go to the PDP.
body: The presenter scores statics on a spectrum. At one end is clarity: the ad says exactly what the product is and why to buy, so the viewer is primed and can land on the product page. At the other end is deliberate curiosity: a short, specific claim with key information withheld ('save $6 a day', with the product blurred), which earns a click and must land on a page that does the explaining, such as a listicle or advertorial. Ads fail in the middle, where the line is vague without being intriguing: his examples are an energy gum headline 'guaranteed energy in just 5 minutes', which raises the obvious 'why not coffee' objection and answers nothing, and a timer brand slogan that reads as confusion rather than mystery. He also flags a common failure: sending curiosity clicks to a standard product page, where the educating the click was promised never happens. How to apply: label every static clear or curious before launch; for curious ones, build or reuse an education-first lander and match its headline to the ad; for clear ones, put the plain benefit first and any science second (he suggests flipping Ketone-IQ's 'lowers ghrelin' to 'feel less hungry' with the mechanism underneath).

fails_when: Retargeting and product-aware audiences, where a plain product-and-offer static is right; brands without capacity to build separate landers for curiosity ads.

claim: For sensitive health problems, an AI or cartoon illustration plus a persona-and-problem headline ('GLP-1 hair loss hits hard') avoids graphic imagery and is cheap to replicate per angle.
body: The last static analysed, from Grüns, is a low-cost template: an AI-generated cartoon illustrating hair loss with the product overlaid and a headline naming a specific persona and problem in as few words as possible, 'GLP-1 hair loss hits hard'. It works on two groups: people on GLP-1 drugs who have hair loss recognise themselves, and those who do not yet start worrying about a side effect they had not heard of, so the problem agitates even people without the symptom. The presenter's reasoning for the cartoon: a real photo of hair loss would be graphic and, in his view, likely to draw higher CPMs or reduced delivery because it leans into a health condition, whereas an illustration shows the problem cleanly. The format is a template: swap the headline and illustration for each core problem the product addresses and you have a series of statics in hours. How to apply: list the specific persona and problem pairs your product solves, write each as a headline of about five to six words, pair it with an illustrated rather than photographic depiction, and launch them as a set to find which problem scales.

claim: Partnership (creator-handle) ads also work as statics: a native tweet-style list of symptoms run through a creator's handle scaled for IM8 without any explicit CTA.
body: Most brands run partnership ads (ads served from a creator's or partner's handle) only as videos. The presenter highlights an IM8 Health static that ran through another account's handle, formatted as a screenshot of a tweet, which viewers do not read as an ad. The headline 'symptoms of vitamin deficiency' self-selects people who care, and the body lists common symptoms (fatigue, dry skin, bleeding gums, bruising) each paired with a vitamin, so a large share of viewers recognise at least one; the post copy then names the product and a 10% code. It reportedly had about 4,700 likes and was scaling. Two lessons: native formats borrowed from organic feeds carry an arbitrage while they are new and lose it as feeds fill with copies; and an ad does not need a printed call to action if the content is convincing, which removes the usual objection to running organic posts as ads. How to apply: test partner-handle statics alongside video, use organic-native layouts (tweet, notes app, text post) for top of funnel, and refresh the format once you see competitors copying it.

claim: A new background colour or pose is not a new ad under Andromeda; change the persona, angle or offer, and scale a winning format by swapping one of those.
body: The agency defines a creative concept as persona plus angle plus offer, optionally plus format. Changing only design details (red to blue background, a different product pose) creates a variation whose effect, perhaps 1 to 2 percent, is too small to measure without very large test budgets and teaches the creative team nothing useful. They report, from Meta reps rather than documentation, that Andromeda now groups near-identical ads under one entity and serves them to the same audience, a response to accounts flooding the system with AI variants, so small tweaks no longer even buy extra reach. How to apply: brief every new static by naming the persona, angle and offer it tests; count it as new only if at least one differs from existing ads. When a format wins (say a problem-agitation static), keep the format and swap one element: a different product, a different persona (women 30 to 40 to men), or a different angle (weight loss to longevity). Use variations sparingly, only to push more spend through a proven concept, with differences large enough to read.

claim: Compare creative types by expected gross profit per ad (revenue minus spend minus production cost); statics cost about a quarter of video, widening the gap at low ROAS.
body: In-platform ROAS ignores what each ad cost to produce. The agency's measure is expected gross profit per ad unit: average revenue per ad, minus average ad spend per ad, minus production cost. Worked example: an ad averages $1,000 revenue at 10x ROAS ($100 spend); a static costing $20 to make leaves $880, a video costing $200 leaves $700. At a more realistic 2x ROAS ($500 spend) the static leaves $480 and the video $300, roughly 40 percent less, even with identical returns. They estimate one good 60 to 90 second video takes the time and money of about three to four statics, and AI tools push static cost toward a dollar or less. Statics also tend to get lower CPMs. How to apply: pull average spend, revenue and lifespan per ad by format from your account, add real production cost per asset, and allocate production budget to the format with the higher expected gross profit; use cheap statics to test new angles, personas and offers, then put proven concepts into costlier video. Use contribution margin instead of revenue when you have it.
conditions: Meta accounts running both statics and video with enough ads per format to compute averages.
fails_when: Categories where video materially outperforms statics on returns (demonstration-heavy products), or compliance-limited accounts; when static averages are inflated by bottom-of-funnel retargeting while video carries prospecting.

claim: Make a static either fully clear or a deliberate curiosity gap, and send curiosity statics to an educational listicle or advertorial, never straight to the product page.
body: The agency sees statics fail in the middle of a spectrum: at one end, maximum clarity, where in three or four seconds the viewer knows the product, angle, persona and offer; at the other, a deliberate curiosity gap such as a native-looking photo, advertorial-style list or problem image that does not reveal the product, pushing the viewer into long primary text or a click. Ads that are half clear and half mysterious neither sell nor drive cheap clicks. Most brands only make clear, product-shot statics, which suit audiences already aware of the product, so statics get typecast as retargeting. Curiosity statics can reach cold, problem-aware or unaware people, but only if the click lands on an education-first page (listicle, advertorial, quiz) or the primary text does the selling; sent to a product page they fail. The image's stage of awareness must match the copy's. Because these top-of-funnel ads hand conversions to follow-up ads, last-click ROAS undercounts them, so judge them on blended business numbers, not in-platform ROAS.

claim: Set monthly ad volume from churn: winners lost per month divided by hit rate; 2 churned winners at a 5 percent hit rate needs about 40 new ads a month.
body: Testing 'as much as possible' wastes budget, because each ad needs enough spend to show whether it works. The agency backs into volume two ways. Churn method: count current winning ads and how many stop working each month, then divide the replacements needed by your historical win rate. Example: 10 winners with 20 percent monthly churn means 2 replacements; at a 5 percent hit rate (they see 5 to 15 percent as normal in large accounts) that is 20 ads per winner, so about 40 new ads a month, assuming quality stays at historical levels. Revenue method: from average spend, ROAS and run time per ad, compute average revenue per ad over its life, then divide the month's revenue target by it to get the number of live ads needed. How to apply: calculate both from the last 90 days of account data and plan production and budget to the higher figure; if the team cannot make that many, the plan is capacity-bound and the target must fall or production must be added. Recompute when hit rate or churn changes.

fails_when: New or small accounts without a reliable hit rate, where the formula gives false precision; accounts where winners rarely churn (evergreen offers), which need far fewer new ads.

claim: A paid hook must filter for buyers, not just stop the scroll, because Meta learns from who keeps watching; broad meme or curiosity hooks train delivery toward non-buyers.
body: The speaker's view is that Meta's delivery still leans on soft signals such as who holds through the first half of a video, even after an ad set passes the roughly 50 conversions that should shift optimisation to purchases. If the opening is an off-topic meme, a satisfying clip or a pure curiosity moment, the people who watch are whoever likes that content, and delivery drifts toward more of them. His example: an educational submarine clip that cut to a snow-removal service reached him in Australia, where it never snows. Organic content can survive this because reach is free, so a few leads from millions of views is still a win; buying the same reach would cost on the order of half a million dollars for those few leads. A jerky ad opening on an ambiguous eating clip had the same flaw: vegetarians watch too. How to apply: put the target persona or their problem on screen or in the first line, make sure the person speaking matches that persona, and judge hooks on clarity and relevance before novelty. Exceptions exist in niches like gaming, where meme openers match the buyer.

claim: Keep the viewer's sense of being sold near zero through the hook and raise it gradually; abrupt jumps from hook to pitch, or education to CTA, cause the biggest drop-offs.
body: Even creators who write good hooks, bodies and calls to action lose viewers at the joins. The speaker plots 'product awareness', the viewer's sense that this is an ad for something, against time: it should sit near zero through the hook and rise slowly to the call to action. Common failures are naming the product in the first sentence (an electrolyte ad that opened by calling the powder the best ever) and step jumps where an educational body suddenly turns into a hard pitch right before the CTA, which he says is where strong creatives most often flop. Better: bridge from the hook into education about the problem (why drinking lots of water does not mean you are hydrated, which minerals matter), mention the product briefly and return to teaching, then let a personal story carry into the offer, such as a creator-partner discount. How to apply: when reviewing retention curves, look for steep drops right after the hook and right before the CTA, and rewrite those transitions so each step gives a reason to keep watching; keep visuals moving through educational sections. Health-claim limits still apply to the reframed angles.

claim: Treat a hook as three separate levers (spoken audio, on-screen text, visual) and grade it on clarity, relevance and novelty first; one script can yield 20 to 30 hooks.
body: Most teams think of the hook as the opening shot. The speaker splits it into the spoken words, the text overlaid on the video (not the ad's primary text) and the visual, and says changing only one can transform results; he cites a case where adding an exaggerated overlay such as 'this transformed my life' roughly doubled hook rate and performance, an anecdote with no sample. Grading order: clarity (would a stranger know what this is about), relevance (is the target's pain obvious), novelty (a new angle or format), then the lesser specificity and credibility. Specific numbers help: 'we taste-tested the bestselling jerky and found the same two problems' should hold better than 'found problems'. Credibility is hard to fit into three seconds unless a known creator or expert is on screen. How to apply: write three or four scripts using different hook types (high-stakes warning, specific proof, contrarian truth, curiosity gap), then pair each with several visuals (cut-aways, product being binned, a whiteboard tease) and overlay lines to get 20 to 30 hooks for one body. Use templates such as persona, problem, pattern interrupt, promise as a start, then move beyond them.
conditions: Video ads on Meta and TikTok where hooks are tested in volume against one body.
fails_when: Low-spend accounts that cannot fund enough impressions per hook to compare them; regulated categories where exaggerated overlays break health-claim rules.

claim: A high-CTR ad can be a false winner: a satisfying-visual ad at 10.9% CTR drove almost no purchases, while a 6.3% CTR routine demo converted; check the CTR-to-link-CTR drop.
body: In a new account spending $30 a day, Meta pushed spend to one visually satisfying ad on day one because its CTR (10.9%, very high for ecommerce), link click-through rate and below-average CPM looked strong. It produced very little buying behaviour: viewers were hooked by the visual but never learned what the product was or why they needed it. A second ad at 6.3% CTR showed the routine, how to apply the product, and a before and after, and it drove purchases. The diagnostic the agency uses is the gap between overall CTR and link CTR: the satisfying ad lost more than 3 percentage points between the two, meaning many who engaged did not go to the site, while the demo ad lost under 2 points, so the people who clicked arrived already primed. Read creative results as a journey: did they stop (hook), did they click (did the ad explain the value), what happened after the click (add to cart, checkout, conversion rate), and can the ad hold spend when budget rises. An ad with good CPA at $30 a day may still fail at scale or suit retargeting better. How to apply: in Ads Manager add CTR (all), link CTR, landing page views and purchases side by side, and do not crown a winner on CTR or on spend share alone.

fails_when: Impulse products where curiosity alone sells, so attention-only creative can convert; single small-sample tests (a few days at $30/day) are directional, not proof.

claim: Set each ad's job by its destination: ads feeding a quiz or listicle only need curiosity plus emotion to earn the click; ads to a product page must sell more.
body: An ad does not have to carry the whole persuasion load when the next step does the selling. If the click goes to a quiz funnel, advertorial or listicle that explains the product, the ad's only job is to stop the scroll, open a curiosity gap and touch the buyer's emotional state, so it can be sparse: a fertility product ad that tells women to stop blaming themselves and take the quiz, or a dark, single-face image with one niche word ('ascend') for a looksmaxxing tool. If the click goes straight to a product page, the ad must also state the benefit, proof and offer, because nothing in between does that work. The emotional register also depends on category: products solving painful problems use fear, insecurity or relief, while low-stakes products (golf club covers, a spit cup for dip users) win on in-group humor and shareability, which also spreads organically when viewers send the ad to friends. How to apply: tag every brief with the destination type and the emotion, then write a brief with six fields: concept, creative type (curiosity static, us versus them, USP callout, review-based), angle and audience, headline, CTA, visual direction. Tracking creative type prevents shipping many near-identical ads.

claim: Once a VSL body works, test 3 to 6 hooks on it, since about 80% of viewers leave during the hook; then test section order and 45-second to 3-minute cuts.
body: In the operator's experience about 80% of viewers never watch past the hook, so the hook is the largest lever once the body and call to action are made. Produce the body once and attach three to six different hooks. Long ads also allow modular edits that short ads do not: move the mechanism before the problem, or bring objection handling or problem agitation earlier, and split-test the orders; he reports good results from rearranging sections. Finally, cut lengths from one script: a 6 to 10 minute VSL can be edited into a 2 to 3 minute version and a 45-second version. He does not think length itself drives much performance, which depends more on the script, but the cuts give the algorithm more distinct variations. Hooks should give a reason to keep watching that is about the viewer's problem, not the brand story. In a long ingredient explanation, also test a faster version, since many viewers will not sit through 30 seconds per ingredient. How to apply: brief editors for the body plus a hook pack, label each modular block so it can be reordered, and request the shorter cuts in the same brief.

claim: Script VSLs as hook, problem in customer words, mechanism, objection handling, proof, risk reversal, CTA; most weak VSLs list what the ingredient is without why it works.
body: The seven parts are: hook; the problem, framed in the customer's own words; the mechanism, which for supplements or consumer goods is the ingredient or technology and why it works; objection handling, covering what the viewer has already tried and why it failed; proof; risk reversal; and a simple call to action. The order can flex: one example went hook, problem, objections, then mechanism. Source the objection section from reviews, support tickets, post-purchase surveys and call notes on why people almost did not buy. The operator's list of common failures: a brand-story hook instead of a problem hook; too much 'what it is' and not enough 'why it matters', so the ad makes claims without a mechanism; weak or buried proof; a vague offer or no CTA; slow pacing and small text, which matters because VSLs skew to older viewers. Comparing two dental-category VSLs, the one with proof, a 90-day guarantee and a clear CTA drew about 25,000 likes; the one with no risk reversal and no CTA drew about 400. A missing CTA can be deliberate when the ad pushes viewers to search on Amazon or relies on retargeting 25% viewers, but for a first VSL include it.

claim: Use long video sales letter ads when conversion is capped by customers not understanding the product: complex, low-trust or new-ingredient categories, sent to a matched landing page, not the PDP.
body: A video sales letter (VSL) ad is a sales argument on video that removes doubt in a set order; it can be 45 to 90 seconds or run 10 to 20 minutes. The operator recommends it for three cases: products that are hard to explain, categories where buyers distrust sellers (supplements are his example), and new categories or ingredients nobody has heard of. The test is whether top-of-funnel conversion is capped because people do not understand the product. If education is needed, it must happen either in the ad or on the landing page, and the strongest setup does both: each VSL angle drives to its own landing page carrying the same message, never a generic product page with no continuity. His example is an Australian supplement account that spent about $360,000 on a single VSL at 2.5 to 3 ROAS on first purchase, with low frequency, which he reads as the ad still reaching new people. The brand accepted that first-order ROAS because retention roughly lifts profit 150% in a customer's first year. How to apply: confirm the education gap with survey or support data, script the VSL, and build a matched page per angle before launch.

A small brand should not copy Nike or Lululemon, whose creative depends on budgets and brand awareness it lacks, nor tiny brands that are not selling. Their rule of thumb: study brands roughly one or two steps above you; if you do $1M a year, look at brands doing about $10M. Within those accounts, ignore low-impression ads and look for ads that have stayed live the longest, since brands rarely keep losing ads running; their example ad had run 469 days. In the Meta Ad Library, a brand may run ads from several pages and pause older ones, so check every page and include inactive ads. Collect the long-running ads by concept (statics, videos, GIFs, carousels), find patterns that recur across several competitors in your category, then build your own version of each concept across your products and make variants. claim: In Petty and Cacioppo's study, agreement peaked at three exposures to the same argument and fell at five; vary the execution rather than repeat one ad.
body: Whitman uses Petty and Cacioppo's 1979 experiment to show that repetition has an optimum. Students heard an argument for higher university spending once, three times or five times. Those exposed three times supported it; at five exposures agreement dropped considerably, which the researchers attributed to tedium turning into counter-arguing against a message that now felt pushy. Repetition builds familiarity and, with it, comfort and trust, and each repeat reaches people who missed earlier ones. But endless repetition of the identical message can create irritation. His distinction: running the same ad over and over is repetitious; running different variations of the same message gets the familiarity benefit without the wear-out. He warns that the lab numbers do not transfer directly to ad frequency, and that an ad still making money should keep running. How to apply on paid social: watch frequency per person on a single creative; when frequency climbs and response falls, rotate a new execution of the same core message (new hook, new person, new format) rather than pushing the same asset harder or abandoning the message.

fails_when: Treating three exposures as a fixed cap: the study used spoken arguments on students, not ads; low-frequency campaigns where wear-out is not the problem; ads still improving with frequency.

claim: Two-sided comparison messages persuade better than one-sided ones only when they both defend your product and rebut the competitor's (Allen, 1991).
body: Whitman cites Allen's 1991 meta-analysis of message sidedness: two-sided messages beat one-sided ones, but only the refutational kind, which acknowledges the other side and then argues against it while advocating your own product. Mentioning the competitor's merits without rebutting them does not win. The mechanism works on both kinds of reader. Skimmers, who judge on surface cues, read a fair-minded message that praises a rival as more credible than ads that only praise themselves. Careful readers, faced with defence plus rebuttal, start questioning the rival's claims. The practical format: credit the competitor briefly and genuinely ('they made the standard for years'), then show why yours is now better on specific benefits (faster, cleaner, cheaper, longer lasting). Comparison charts that set your advantages side by side are singled out as especially effective for low-effort readers, who treat the chart as research already done for them. Related tactic: telling people who should not buy raises credibility and sharpens desire among real prospects. How to apply: in us-versus-them ads and on comparison sections of product pages, include one fair concession, then a clear rebuttal and a chart; avoid pure bashing.
conditions: Categories with known incumbents; considered purchases where shoppers compare options; comparison sections on product or landing pages.
fails_when: Claims about competitors you cannot substantiate (ad policy and comparative advertising law); naming a competitor in markets where that is restricted; a two-sided message with no rebuttal, which can push buyers to the rival.

claim: Swipe video formats from outside your niche, not from competitors, by logging beginning, middle and end for location, pacing, script, on-screen text, lighting and viewer feeling.
body: Copying a competitor's winning story usually fails, the founder argues, because it reaches the audience that has already been served that story; the platform has nowhere new to put it. A new angle or format finds an underserved pocket, which is why new often outperforms safe. His method, 'frame swiping', borrows structure from viral videos in other categories. Build a table with rows for the beginning, middle and end of the reference video and columns for location and visuals, pacing (how fast the cuts are), audio and script including trigger words, on-screen text, lighting (which sets tone and is often missed) and what the viewer feels at that point. His teardown of a teeth-whitening ad: it opens on an influencer clip calling the product a rip-off in a warehouse (viewer: curious), switches to fast GoPro point-of-view cuts revealing the influencer used a counterfeit (viewer: worried about buying a fake), and ends with the genuine product working plus a bundle offer. A clothing or homeware brand can reuse that exact rhythm with its own product. Keep cuts tight: pauses of a fraction of a second lose viewers. claim: Keep one ad on one awareness stage, or move downward steadily; a product-aware image with solution-aware copy fails both groups, and abrupt product 'bridges' lose viewers.
body: The five stages: unaware (does not know the problem exists, needs a bold claim and reframe), problem-aware (knows the problem, open to agitation), solution-aware (knows solutions exist, needs your unique mechanism), product-aware (knows you, needs proof, risk reversal and offer clarity, roughly site visitors) and most-aware (about to buy, roughly add-to-carts). The operator's rule: an ad either sits on one stage or starts high and pulls the viewer steadily down through the stages. What fails is a blend, such as a static image that only makes sense if you know the product, paired with copy explaining what creatine does; it resonates with neither group. A quick test of stage is how early the product appears: one shorts ad introduced the product about 9 seconds in, which places it around solution-aware. In video, keep the viewer's sense of being sold to low through the hook and body and let it rise gradually to the CTA; a 'staircase' that drops in the product, wanders back to problem talk, then pitches again shows up as retention drops. Statics are not only for retargeting: unaware statics with an intriguing image and long story-led primary text can spend about $250,000 and run for months.

claim: Put about 80% of creative volume in unaware and problem-aware ads, 10% solution-aware, 10% product and most aware; product-aware-heavy accounts stay warm and frequency climbs.
body: The operator's diagnosis for broad Meta campaigns that will not scale: most brands write ads as if everyone already knows the product, leading with features, ingredients and price, while most people are problem-aware at best. Since the Andromeda delivery changes, Meta reads the creative and serves it to the people it suits, so a pile of product-aware ads is kept on the small warm pool that converts on them. As budget rises, Meta keeps serving the same warm people and frequency climbs. Adding website-visitor exclusions does not fix it, he argues, because the ads do not work on cold people and the system knows it. The fix is the creative mix: about 80% of new creative aimed at unaware and problem-aware people, about 10% at solution-aware, about 10% at product-aware and most-aware, adjusted if retargeting underperforms or a stage overperforms. Product-aware ads grouped in an ad set will retarget on their own; most-aware needs little more than a catalogue ad. Expect top-of-funnel ads to show weaker attributed ROAS while lifting conversions credited elsewhere, so judge them on account-wide results. Direct-response marketers had run that style on native ad networks for decades; when it became widely discussed among ecommerce marketers, he saw its performance decline across many accounts he had access to, as more advertisers flooded the feed with the same look and the novelty that made it stand out was lost. His underlying principle is contrast: study what competitors and creators in your niche are doing and make your ads look different, while still not looking like an ad (Gary Halbert's direct mail made to look like personal letters is his historical example). claim: Black Friday results corrupt creative analysis: judge ads at ad-set level and lean on CTR and CPC, since ad ROAS mostly reflects which product was discounted.
body: The period that generates the most data is also the least reliable for learning which creative works. Blue Sense Digital's rule for Black Friday: judge creative at the ad set level rather than the individual ad, because Meta optimises across multiple touches while reporting last click, and the breakdown effect makes ad-level ROAS especially misleading. In this window only, lean more on creative metrics such as CTR and CPC. Outside the sale they say the opposite: across large data sets CPC shows no meaningful correlation with ROAS (very low R-squared), so it should not be used to judge ads year-round. claim: Size Black Friday creative from per-ad spend ceilings: winners hold about $8k to $13k AUD a day, so a $150k peak day needs 12 to 18 such ads.
body: Creative is often the constraint at Black Friday spend levels. Blue Sense Digital's method: look at last November's peak daily spend per ad. In their AUD accounts the highest single ad reached about $12,500 a day; most evergreen ads spent about $4,000 to $8,500; a realistic working ceiling for a winner is about $8,000 to $13,000, so plan around $10,000 to $12,000 for winners and about $5,000 for an average evergreen ad. claim: Scale a single multi-benefit SKU by running separate angle pillars for different buyer groups, each with its own landing page, since every angle hits a spend ceiling.
body: The speaker's read of Grüns' Meta Ad Library: about 660 live ads for one gummy product, grouped into pillars (gut health, GLP-1 support, daily multivitamin, fiber, hair health, energy, immunity, cognition), many run as partnership ads. Mechanism: each angle reaches a limited pool of people who have that specific problem, so spend on any one angle tops out; adding pillars adds separate pools, letting one SKU absorb far more spend. The alternative most brands take, launching new SKUs to reach new buyers, ties cash up in inventory, risks discounting failed launches, and adds 3PL and operating complexity; one SKU keeps cash flow lean. Two rules make it work. First, each angle should target a genuinely different person (social drinkers, people noticing first grey hairs, gamers, entrepreneurs), not ten hooks aimed at the same group. Second, the click must land on a page built for that angle: Grüns sends GLP-1 ads to a page about GLP-1 support benefits, because a hyper-specific ad that lands on a generic 20-benefit product page makes buyers wonder whether they need the whole product. The speaker uses a reasoning-mode LLM prompt to generate 10 to 15 angles, each with audience, hook and reason it works, then builds pages for the one or two that win.
conditions: Single-SKU or few-SKU brands whose product genuinely serves several jobs (multi-ingredient supplements, versatile consumables); Meta spend large enough to hit angle ceilings; ability to build angle-specific landing pages or advertorials.

claim: IM8 scales one winning 'clock' script (day 1, 9, 21: ingredient, dose, scene) by swapping only the persona, and plans volume at about $2,500 spend per ad.
body: After transcribing every active IM8 video ad, the speaker found one dominant long-form structure. It opens with a symptom hook for a single persona, reframes the cause, then walks a timeline (on day one you notice this, by day 9 this, after 21 days this), naming a specific ingredient and dose at each checkpoint, describing outcomes as scenes rather than claims (playing with grandkids instead of fixes arthritis), and ending with proof, then offer, guarantee and scarcity. The timeline works as a retention device, like teasing what is coming in a YouTube video. The angle and offer stay fixed while the persona changes: joints, menopause, GLP-1 users, regular drinkers, gut and bloating, each with near-identical script lines adapted in language, and each driven to a matching persona landing page. Creative volume tracks spend almost linearly; the speaker estimates each ad holds about $2,500 of spend, so doubling budget means doubling ad count. In a 40-ad sample, most sat at problem and solution aware, with few unaware ads and one most-aware and three product-aware. Claims got more aggressive in unaware ads (kidney symptoms, antidepressant comparisons), where regulatory exposure concentrates. How to apply: once a script wins, list your top personas and remake it per persona before inventing new concepts.

claim: Smoke-test angles with one product-on-white image and a bold text bar, changing only the value prop; expand the winning angle into video, then test who appears.
body: The guest's first test with a small budget, which he calls a smoke test: take the easiest asset to make, the product on a white background with a white bar of bold call-out text, and run near-identical versions where only the text changes, one per value proposition (his fidget spinner example: reduce anxiety, increase focus, relieve stress). Whichever gets the most clicks and engagement at acceptable cost wins the angle. The next step is a longer explanatory video on that angle, then variations on who is shown: a man, a woman, both, or only hands and arms, which he uses so viewers can picture themselves without rejecting a face that does not look like them. The system repeats as winners emerge, getting more granular by creator, colour or region; he notes ads featuring people who look local to a state perform better there. Read the funnel in order: if CPM and click costs are normal for the niche (he cites $15 to $30 CPMs depending on audience) but people abandon at cart, the price or offer is wrong, so test price before more creative.

claim: True Classic cuts every ad with 4 to 5 different openers (6 for a comedy parody) because the first 3 seconds decide thumb-stop rate and taste is unreliable.
body: Bartlett says the opener is the whole game: if viewers are not hooked in the first 3 seconds, they never reach the message. So every True Classic ad ships with 4 to 5 alternative openers, and their recent movie-parody comedy ad had six, because what the team finds funny may not land with customers. The approach is iteration within existing content: one body, many first-3-second variants, then find the winner and build on it. Their creative mix pairs comedy parodies for brand reach with direct-response side-by-side comparisons that prove the fit claim (their fitted shirt next to a baggy generic one), which they also put on the home page instead of lifestyle images. He insists creative must reach an internal 8 out of 10 before release and says agencies often deliver a 6. claim: Fix a video ad's first half first: only about 15% of viewers reach the second half, so reveal the product late and state benefits before features.
body: Across six Meta ads, the presenter's pattern was that winners delay the product and losers lead with it. A weak ad opened with 'these are my vital packs': no problem, no reason to care, and the value proposition arrived 7 to 10 seconds in. Because retention only falls over the length of an ad, he estimates only about 15% of viewers see the second half, so a strong ending cannot rescue a weak opening, while a strong opening can carry an average ending. Structure he credits in the winners: a high-stakes or curiosity hook aimed at the right buyer, a bridge that says a solution exists without naming the product, objection handling, category-level authority (for example a hat design centuries old), then a soft call to action. Cuts happen at least every three seconds. When features appear, state the lifestyle benefit first and the feature as the reason ('I can nap for 30 minutes mid-day because the armrests drop and the fabric is soft'), so more of the shrinking audience hears the benefit. Two failure modes: a hook that grabs attention through confusion attracts the wrong viewers, and a founder-authority ad with no on-screen proof only converts people who already trust the founder.

fails_when: Retargeting or warm audiences who already know the product, where an early product reveal and offer can work; partnership ads on a creator's page where the creator's credibility is the hook.

claim: Near-duplicate ads get grouped under one Meta entity ID and serve to the same users: 200 similar ads might count as about 20 unique ads, adding no new reach.
body: Meta's retrieval stage (Andromeda), extended by GEM to read video, audio and format, scans every ad and groups creatives it judges to be the same. Grouped ads share one entity ID, so in the presenter's example 200 ads uploaded as small variations might register as only about 20 unique ads, and every ad inside a group serves to the same pool of people. Extra variations then add cost and noise but no unique reach, which defeats the purpose of creative volume: reaching new people or giving existing viewers a genuinely new reason to buy. How to apply: plan creative by concept, defined as the intersection of angle, offer and persona, and treat format as a fourth axis because a big enough format change (static versus UGC video versus founder talking head) can register as a different ad even with the same message. Iterations (new hooks, colours, edits) still have a place for optimising a winning concept, but count your new-reach pipeline in concepts, not ad count. When reach stalls and frequency climbs, check how many distinct concepts are actually live before adding more variants. Broad targeting makes this matter more, because the creative itself now decides which user clusters see the ad.
conditions: Meta Advantage+ or broad-targeted accounts on the current Andromeda-era delivery system; any spend level running many creatives.
fails_when: Small accounts with only a few ads, where the bottleneck is spend or offer, not uniqueness; the 200-to-20 figure is illustrative, not a measured ratio.

claim: After Andromeda, still test hook variations: launch each net-new concept as its own ad set with about 3 variations, because a variation often wins where the original loses.
body: A popular reading of the Andromeda update is that advertisers should only launch net-new concepts and stop making variations. This media buyer disagrees. His launch structure: each ad set holds one net-new concept, and the ads inside it are the original plus variations of that concept, typically different hooks (for example one concept with three hooks). The variations are extra attempts at the same idea; in his experience one of them is often the winner while the original concept ad loses, so killing variations would have wrongly written off a concept that works. What rarely works is making variations of the account's existing top ad in the hope of beating it: they tend to perform decently but not better. Combine this with the entity-ID point that very similar ads collapse together: the variation should change something the viewer notices first (the hook, opening visual or framing), not just colours or end cards. How to apply: count tests at the concept level, give each concept a few hook variations, judge the concept by its best variation, and then build new concepts rather than endlessly re-cutting the current winner.
conditions: Meta accounts launching new creative weekly on broad or Advantage+ delivery; ecommerce creative testing.
fails_when: Very low budgets where splitting spend across several variations per concept leaves each with too little delivery to judge; variations so similar they share an entity ID.

claim: Test 4 or 5 angles by changing only the ad headline to one product page, then rewrite the page top around the winner; one brand reportedly tripled in a month.
body: The founder's sequence for a product that is not selling well: before rebuilding the site or changing the product, write four or five distinct angles. Run the same ad with only the headline or hook changed for each angle, all pointing to the same existing product page, so the angle is the only variable. Then change the landing page to match: the top-of-page imagery, headline and copy are rebuilt around the winning angle so the ad's promise continues on the page. He says one brand tripled its revenue in a month from this alone, then the team made many more creatives on that angle. He treats this as the step most founders skip in favour of small conversion tweaks, and uses it to diagnose product-market fit: if several angles and demographics all still struggle to sell, the issue is probably the product or positioning, not the ads.
